summary: William Kantrowitz complains again, following RFC 459, about the many requests for information that ARPANET sites receive, such as host charts that duplicate the Resource Notebook and requests for hourly load numbers. It is an opinion piece. It updates RFC 459.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 514 objects to requests that make network sites collect and send information. Its author argues that requesters should explain why the work is needed and how much time it will take.

subtitle: A complaint about repeated information requests burdening small network sites.

tldr.problem: Kantrowitz says network sites were being asked for overlapping host information, computer-load figures and program listings, creating extra work.
tldr.mechanism: He gives examples, questions the value and cost of a proposed central program repository, and asks requesters to justify the work they want others to do.
tldr.outcome: This is an opinion piece, not a protocol. The author refers back to the plea in RFC 459.

today: The unit records RFC 514's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The document refers back to the author's plea in RFC 459.

sections.title: Examples of Extra Work
sections.content:
Kantrowitz lists three recent requests that he sees as make-work. A set of host charts duplicated information already in the Resource Notebook and would require maintaining two documents. A caller requested hourly TX-2 computer-load figures for April and May. A message about a central software repository and personnel file prompted this RFC.

The attached message asks sites to send available programs and documentation, including descriptions, listings, operating instructions and limitations. It also asks for information about staff with particular technical skills.
sections.plainLanguage: The author describes repeated requests for host details, computer-load figures, program copies and staff information. He says these requests create work for the sites that must answer them.

sections.title: The Cost of Listing Every Program
sections.content:
The RFC focuses on the idea of listing every program available to network users. Kantrowitz asks how much paper the listings would produce, who would use the complete collection, and whether sites would need to send a new listing whenever a program changed.

He notes that many TX-2 programs are written in assembly language and asks whether the site would also need to provide its assembly-language manual and operating-system listings. He says these issues are more acute for a site with only one computer.
sections.plainLanguage: Listing every program could require much more material than a program's name. The author questions whether the resulting collection would be useful enough to justify the effort.

sections.title: Ask Whether the Work Is Worthwhile
sections.content:
Kantrowitz repeats his plea from RFC 459 not to overwhelm small research sites with administrative tasks. He recalls that TX-2 and SDC had conducted early experiments with a small-scale network prototype that helped lead to the ARPA Network, and argues that sites need time to do useful work.

His advice to future requesters is to justify the request, estimate the time it will take others, explain why they might be motivated to help, and review the request with colleagues before sending it.
sections.plainLanguage: Before asking other sites to do work, explain why it matters and how much time it will take. The author argues that this can help protect time for research.

references.text: Kantrowitz, W., RFC 459, the earlier plea mentioned in this document.
Marill, T. and Roberts, L., Toward a Cooperative Network of Time-Shared Computers, AFIPS Conference Proceedings, November 1966.
